first_impression.reaction: Our daughter sent this with 'Mum, read this before you ring me', so I did, top to bottom on the iPad. The first paragraph answered the thing I was actually worried about: the pretty ceremony overseas doesn't make them married on its own, and the legal part can be done here at home. That's a relief, because I don't fancy anyone signing papers in Italian. It's calm, plain and quotes the government, which I like. What it doesn't do is say a word about deposits, contracts, or Mum and her walking frame. Fair enough, it's a page about ceremonies, but those are my questions.

journey.quote: A symbolic ceremony is a wedding ceremony with no legal effect.
journey.reaction: Straight to the point. Now I understand what she meant on the phone. I can forward this first paragraph to Geoff as it is.

journey.quote: A common route is a small legal ceremony in Australia and a symbolic ceremony at the destination for the celebration itself.
journey.reaction: That sounds the most sensible to me. Australian law, Australian celebrant, paperwork in English. Less to go wrong.

journey.quote: General information as at November 2026, not legal advice.
journey.reaction: Good. Dated and honest about what it is. I trust that more than someone pretending to be a lawyer.

journey.section: What makes a wedding legal in Australia
journey.quote: The words are set out in the Act.
journey.reaction: Then two long quotes from the Act with 'thee' in them. I read them because I read everything, but I don't need the exact wording, the celebrant does. It slowed me down.

journey.section: How to Marry Legally and Still Have a Symbolic Ceremony
journey.quote: Either way, decide the route before you pay deposits, because it shapes your timeline, your celebrant and what you tell guests.
journey.reaction: Yes. The first mention of money, and it's the right advice: decide before anything is paid. That's what I'd say to her.

journey.section: Marry legally in Australia, celebrate abroad
journey.quote: Some couples do this before they fly and others after they come home; talk your dates through with your celebrant against the notice window.
journey.reaction: Clear enough. And it makes me think: if the legal bit is here in Melbourne, Mum can be at that one without a long flight. That matters to us.

journey.quote: DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their own country, so ask the embassy or consulate whether you need one, where to get it, and whether it needs an authentication or apostille.
journey.reaction: This whole paragraph is one long run of acronyms and 'ask the embassy'. I followed it, just, but it's exactly the sort of foreign paperwork I'd worry the children would get wrong, and the page leaves them to do it alone.

journey.quote: Check with your state or territory registry before you rely on it.
journey.reaction: Useful. I'd never have thought the name change could be a problem. That alone pushes me towards the legal ceremony at home.

journey.quote: Who do we want at the legal ceremony, if it is separate?
journey.reaction: Me, for one. And Mum. Nice that it's asked, it treats family as part of this.

journey.section: Questions for the venue and celebrant
journey.quote: What time does the ceremony start, is there a rehearsal, and what is the wet weather plan?
journey.reaction: Good practical list. But nothing on whether Mum can get to a clifftop terrace, and nothing on whose name is on the contract or when the deposit is gone. Those are the two I'd add before I'd let anyone sign.

journey.section: Questions for the venue and celebrant
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor confirms venue inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: In writing, before we commit. That's the line I was waiting for. I'd still like to know who that Advisor is and whether I can speak to them.

journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor stays with you from start to finish as a single point of contact, planning the venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world.
journey.reaction: One person, including the payments. That's the accountability I want when it's our money. But no mention of a phone call, or of who answers if something goes wrong on the night.

unanswered_questions: Who do we ring if something goes wrong on the wedding weekend, after hours, Italian time? Is someone from Wedded Wonderland there on the day? (deferred business detail)
Is the first conversation a phone call with a real person, and can I join it as the parent paying half?
How is the Wedded Advisor's fee charged and agreed, and is it in writing in AUD? (fees deferred)
Are our deposits with an overseas venue protected if the venue or a supplier fails?
Does Wedded Wonderland help with any of the legal paperwork, or is that entirely the couple and their celebrant? (the page implies the couple handles it; I'd like it said plainly)
Does the Advisor check that ceremony spaces are accessible for an elderly guest with a walking frame, and arrange transfers? (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: Documents come from the destination's rules. Some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married, with a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages as the common documents, and a country may have more rules, such as a residence period.
turn_offs_found.why: Not a tone problem, but this paragraph and the DFAT one run together into a long, dense block of paperwork terms on the iPad. That's the 'long unbroken paragraph' I struggle with, and it's the one bit I most needed to follow.

would_share_with: My husband: the intro and the 'decide the route before you pay deposits' line, so he knows the legal side can be done at home
My daughter: the name change line and the questions for the venue, so she asks them before signing anything

cta_reaction.quote: A Wedded Advisor stays with you from start to finish as a single point of contact, planning the venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world.
cta_reaction.why: Single point of contact and payments handled is the right promise for me. But I'd talk to Geoff first, and I'd only go further if the first step is a phone call with a named person who can tell me how deposits and contracts work and who is there on the day.

top_3_changes: Add a contracts and deposits question to the venue list (a question, not a claim). Old: "- What time does the ceremony start, is there a rehearsal, and what is the wet weather plan?" New: "- What time does the ceremony start, is there a rehearsal, and what is the wet weather plan?\n- Whose name is on the contract, in which currency are payments made, and when do deposits become non-refundable?"

Add an accessibility question to the same list (a question, not a claim). Old: "- Which rituals and props are allowed: sand, candles, open flame, confetti?" New: "- Which rituals and props are allowed: sand, candles, open flame, confetti?\n- Is there level access to the ceremony space for older guests or anyone with limited mobility?"

Break the dense CNI paragraph in two so it reads on a tablet; no wording change. Old: "The destination's embassy or consulate is the place to ask. <!-- fact_17 --> DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia," New: "The destination's embassy or consulate is the place to ask. <!-- fact_17 -->\n\nDFAT can issue a CNI in Australia,"

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft (visible text only, link markup stripped)
Stayed in character as Margaret, funding parent, reading top to bottom on an iPad after her daughter sent the link
No invented brand facts; on-the-day support, fees, deposit protection, paperwork help, accessibility checks and transfers placed in unanswered_questions
Suggested edits are exact old/new strings, add only questions or a paragraph break, and introduce no new facts or legal claims
Suggestions stay within brand limits: nothing on fees, commissions, supplier sourcing or vetting, or the brand handling legal paperwork
HTML comments and VERIFY markers treated as invisible

open_questions.question: The draft never says who handles the legal paperwork. Should the page state plainly that the couple and their celebrant handle it (the brand does not), so a paying parent isn't left guessing? Wording would need approval, as it is a brand statement.

Can the business confirm whether the first Concierge step is a phone call with a named Advisor? If so, saying so near the closing CTA would lift parents' likelihood to enquire. If not confirmed, leave as is.

assumptions: Margaret arrived via a link from her daughter, reading on an iPad, contributing about half. Relevance is 3 because this is a ceremony and legal explainer written to the couple, not a money or logistics page.

Likelihood to enquire is 3: 'decide the route before you pay deposits', 'in writing' and 'single point of contact... payments' earn trust, but no phone call, named person or on-the-day help is mentioned. Those are deferred business details and are not treated as must-fix.
Husband's name (Geoff) and the walking frame are character colour from the persona card and earlier panels, not page facts.
Fast mode: full article read top to bottom, FAQ skimmed as it repeats the body.
